À qui profitent réellement les ruelles v: Who Really Benefits From Green Alleys?
« Pour nous, les gens qui habitent en vi: “For those of us who live in the city, it’s also a way of connecting with nature.”
Lorsqu’on se promène dans les rues de Mo: Walking through the streets of Montréal, you may come across alleyways between ordinary intersections. Venture into one, and you find yourself surrounded by greenery, between vegetable planters and flowering shrubs. “It’s like a little corner of paradise,” Louisa tells La Converse. A permanent resident who has lived in Quebec since 2020, the woman in her seventies considers Montréal’s green alleys a “breath of relief” amid the cacophony of the city.
Depuis 1995, des ruelles vertes ont été: Since 1995, green alleys have been gradually developed in Montréal for a range of purposes: increasing biodiversity in the city to promote the ecological transition, creating safer neighbourhoods and encouraging inclusivity by providing a gathering place for the neighbourhood. This type of citizen initiative, strongly encouraged by the City and its boroughs, involves transforming existing alleys into green spaces by adding elements such as flower planters, for example, or plenty of shrubs and trees. The City of Montréal has committed to greening these small alleyways in a cooperative effort with residents. But who actually benefits from these green alleys?
Un panneau signalant une ruelle verte da: A sign marking a green alley in the Mile-End neighbourhood. Photo: Rin Eadie
Paula Selcado a 22 ans et fréquente asse: Paula Selcado is 22 and often visits the green alley near her home. “I’ve lived in Hochelaga since I came to Quebec. There’s one right next to my place. It’s a very calm and pleasant spot. I sometimes go there to study or read. I always sit in the same spot, in the shade,” she begins. A university student, she also uses her neighbourhood’s green alleys to study in peace and quiet. She stresses how important such a place is in the middle of a neighbourhood she considers busy. “A green space like that is necessary. Especially in the liveliest neighbourhoods, where there’s more coming and going. It gives residents a place where they can escape their daily lives, relax in the city.” Smiling, she adds: “There are even kids who go play there sometimes. It’s safe enough for them to spend their time there.”
« Pour nous, les gens qui habitent en vi: “For those of us who live in the city, it’s also a way of connecting with nature.” Having left the Dominican Republic at the age of seven, Paula has known only Montréal and its busy streets since. Apart from the rare times she’s able to leave the city to travel, she doesn’t get much chance to retreat into nature. “Even if it’s in the middle of the city, it’s still a green space. We take advantage of it as best we can. For me, it’s really an escape.”
Malgré son affection pour les ruelles ve: Despite her fondness for green alleys, Paula sees them somewhat as a “poisoned gift.” “I’m lucky. I live in a neighbourhood where these spaces exist for us to enjoy. But I’m aware that not all Montrealers can enjoy these places,” she admits. Indeed, despite the City of Montréal’s efforts to sustainably develop biodiversity, green alleys are not available in every borough. Twelve of the city’s 19 boroughs have developed at least one, and most of them are concentrated in central neighbourhoods: La Petite-Patrie, Rosemont, the Mile End and the Plateau, among others.
Selon Paula, ce projet de verdissement u: According to Paula, this urban greening project is a solution for some, but given the uneven distribution of green spaces, it is also a source of inequality for others. “The rollout of green alleys seems to have everything going for it. It creates a calm, pleasant space for the neighbourhood, and it makes the area safer. But what I’ve noticed is that they’re only in certain parts of the city. The CEGEP and the high school I attended were in the Saint-Michel neighbourhood, and I never saw, or even thought I’d see, anything like a green alley there.” Thinking about it a little more, she adds that “when you think about the green alley project, you don’t picture a recently immigrated family who doesn’t speak French or English well enjoying it; you don’t think of a green alley project in Little Maghreb or in Parc-Extension,” she says. “Unfortunately, in my view, green alleys are a symptom of gentrification.”
<strong>La ruelle verte comme échappatoi: The green alley as an escape and a place to socialize
Si le projet d’aménagement des ruelles v: While the green alley project seems to Paula like a symptom of social inequality, others see it as a necessary development for building a healthy metropolis. That is the case for Louisa Ferrad, who has been in Montréal for just over three years now, and for whom green alleys are one of the last bridges connecting her to her life in Algeria.
« Lorsque j’ai quitté mon Algérie, j’ai: “When I left my Algeria, I left my home, my mountain, my house,” Louisa begins. Having grown up in a village at the foot of a mountain, the 74-year-old new Montrealer says she is fascinated by the city’s green alleys. “The first time I came across a green alley was a few years ago. I had come to visit my daughter in Montréal and I was thinking about settling here.” But her enthusiasm for a new life in North America dropped abruptly when she realized the differences between life in the Algerian countryside and life in a Montréal neighbourhood. “Here, everything is calculated. There are traffic lights at almost every corner; there are huge numbers of cars, cyclists, motorcycles, trucks, and so on. Everything is paved, everything is always under renovation, everything moves fast. Apart from the parks, I don’t have access to green spaces,” Louisa laments.
Malgré ce choc culturel, la septuagénair: Despite this culture shock, the woman in her seventies changed her mind, driven by the desire to be with her daughter, who has lived in Montréal for more than 10 years. In July 2020, she obtained her permanent residence. She left her house and her mountain. “[Here], my daughter has a small yard behind her place; we plant a few vegetables, a few herbs. It’s nice, but when I remember that in Algeria, I had lemon trees and fig trees as far as the eye could see behind our house, it breaks my heart,” she continues. “When I came back to Montréal, the alley where the neighbourhood kids played had been transformed. Located in the Rosemont–La Petite-Patrie borough, it’s now dotted with planters and shrubs. There’s even a little fence to protect the flowers that were planted there. The kids can also play there more safely, since there are even signs saying the alley is used by young children!”
Louisa est une aînée, et elle ne travail: Louisa is a senior, and she doesn’t work. Unable to read or write, she is currently learning French, even though she gets by quite well orally and has no great difficulty communicating. The green alley has been, in a way, a means of integrating into her new environment and her new neighbourhood. “When I came here, I didn’t know anyone, except my daughter and her little family. Then I started spending time in the alley behind our home. I became friends with one of the neighbours. She was Moroccan, she spoke to me in Arabic, and that sped up our bond. Now, everyone in the building knows me. Sometimes I look after my neighbours’ kids, people bring me food from time to time, and we have barbecues and picnics all together. If the alley hadn’t been developed, I wouldn’t have had a place to spend my free time. I wouldn’t have had people to meet, I would simply have been bored,” she concludes.
Les enjeux sociaux et environnementaux a: For many residents of neighbourhoods with green alleys, the main positives of these projects are the social and environmental benefits, as well as neighbourhood safety and upkeep. But they also reveal problems tied to rising rents.
Délicia Raza habite l’arrondissement du: Délicia Raza lives in the Plateau-Mont-Royal borough. For this 24-year-old resident, green alleys contribute significantly to Montréal’s current housing crisis. “A green alley, when it’s well maintained, makes the neighbourhood more desirable. It makes it safer, prettier; so it drives up the price of the housing around it,” she begins. “In my neighbourhood, you can see several really well-designed green alleys. And when I tell people I live in the Plateau-Mont-Royal, the reaction is often the same: ‘You live in a gentrified neighbourhood,’” she exclaims. In her view, green alleys widen the disparities between communities in Montréal. “I don’t remember ever seeing green alleys in certain neighbourhoods, and I get the impression that life and community in those neighbourhoods are less vibrant compared to what you see elsewhere, like on the Plateau for example. Green alleys contribute to community life, and the fact that there aren’t any in some places accentuates the marginalization of the residents of those neighbourhoods.”
L’emplacement des ruelles vertes est don: The location of green alleys has therefore become a criterion for the quality of life of housing. When they are near a property or a unit for rent, they are reportedly taken into account when it comes to the cost of living. “When I tell people what I pay per month for a 3½ in the Plateau-Mont-Royal, they’re surprised. I was lucky, I pay a relatively low amount compared to what a similar rental can cost in my neighbourhood. Before I came across my place, I could clearly see that apartments near green spaces tended to be more sought after, and so more expensive. And if there are neighbourhoods with far more green spaces than others, then living there costs more. The less well-off residents end up isolated, and that’s how the disparity is created,” Délicia concludes.

Manal Tachfine est étudiante en urbanism: Manal Tachfine is an urban planning student at the Université du Québec à Montréal. Also holding a college technical diploma in the field, she says that “the green alley has several advantages over the ordinary alley we already have in Montréal.” “Not only does it create vitality, but it also helps fight the heat islands that build up as more and more of the territory gets paved,” she adds. She says that, in theory, the idea of green alleys is an excellent solution for a metropolis like Montréal, where urbanization keeps growing.
Elle évoque également le côté agréable d: She also points to how pleasant these alleys are. “It’s welcoming and warm, it lets neighbours use them as meeting places. Rather than going to the park and having to travel there, you can bring that vitality to where you are.”
Dans les quartiers un peu plus défavoris: In somewhat more disadvantaged neighbourhoods, it would be more beneficial to develop more green alleys, the expert believes. “Outlying neighbourhoods like Saint-Léonard or Montréal-Nord have almost no green alleys, or none at all, even though, geographically speaking, there are more accessible alleys there than in other neighbourhoods.” She also speaks about the community character of these spaces. “The alleys are used extremely heavily by children, and so by residents, especially in these boroughs. For the well-being of these residents, it would be good to promote the development of these green alleys in neighbourhoods that are somewhat more isolated from the city centre,” she concludes.
<strong>Montréal, où la disparité géogra: Montréal, where geographic disparity continues to call the shots
<l1>Dans une ville où l’espérance de vie: <l1>In a city where life expectancy varies depending on the neighbourhood you live in</l1>, the question of geographic disparity is central. Since its launch in the metropolis in 1995, the Ruelles vertes project has aimed to be both restorative and innovative, for a greener, safer and healthier Montréal. Despite that aim, people like Paula, Louisa and Délicia all have different experiences of, and relationships with, these unique alleyways.
Lorsqu’on remarque que ces espaces sont: When you notice that these spaces are mainly concentrated in neighbourhoods where quality of life and safety are higher than in others, it makes sense that those who don’t frequent these places would question why they’ve been left out of such a community project. Recently, after a finding that there was a lack of green space in the east end of the island of Montréal, a pilot project to set up green alleys was launched in the Rivière-des-Prairies–Pointe-aux-Trembles borough. Residents quickly volunteered to help develop these spaces.
